pages.text:
Saturday sixty-one started with a hug.

I walked into the kitchen where Dad was fanning the smoke alarm, and I did not walk past him. I wrapped my arms around his middle, right over the cartoon fish apron. He froze. Then he hugged me back, hard enough to squeeze the air out of my lungs.

"Dad," I said. "Tell me about Ohio."

He blinked. "What? I just told you about the book."

"No," I said. "About this. The neighbors. The street. What you loved here before you started making puns to cover your nerves."

He looked at me for a long time. Then he started talking. He talked for twenty minutes. He talked about the smell of cut grass in July and the way the light hit the cornfields at dusk. His eyes got shiny. He told me about the time he fixed Mr. Grady’s sprinkler and felt like a hero for about five seconds.

At 6:47 the next morning, Gus roared in my face.

Dad was in the kitchen, burning toast again. He looked at me with a blank, cheerful face. He did not remember the light. He did not remember the cornfields. He just made the anti-gravity pun.

I went to Mom next. I made her pancakes and brought them to her bed with a list called NOTHING TO WORRY ABOUT. She cried happy tears.

At 6:47, she was back to the clipboard.
pages.image: Max stands in a kitchen doorway hugging a tall man in a fish apron while smoke swirls around them; the man looks tearful and surprised, holding a dish towel; warm morning light.

pages.text:
Saturdays sixty-two through sixty-six were for Tessa.

I knew exactly what she was scared of. It was being a nobody in a new school. So I went to Jonah’s sister to borrow her drum kit. She said yes. Probably because I looked like I was about to cry. I didn’t argue when she asked why.

On Saturday sixty-three, I carried the kit to Larkspur Park. My shoulders burned under the weight. It felt like carrying a full refrigerator of hot soup. I set it up by the big oak tree.

I tapped on the snare drum until Tessa came out. She stopped. She looked at the drums. Then she looked at me.

I just said, "Play."

She played for an hour. She hit the cymbals so hard the feathers on the snare drum flew into the grass. She smiled a big, real smile. It was the kind that crinkles the eyes.

I watched from the fence. I felt like I had built a bridge out of nothing.

Then 6:47 came.

The drums were back in the box. Tessa was in her room. The smile had been packed away with the rest of the day.
pages.image: Tessa, a girl with a purple hair streak and headphones, sits on a bench in a park playing a small drum kit; she is smiling broadly; Max stands by a wooden fence watching her, hands in his hoodie pockets.

pages.text:
Saturday sixty-seven was the crash.

I had spent six Saturdays preparing Tessa for the drums. I had organized the kit. I had timed the practice. I made sure the park was clear of squirrels.

At 10:30, I walked into the garage. Tessa was standing in front of the box of posters. She looked at me. She did not see the drums. She did not see the park. She saw her brother, and she saw the fight we were about to have.

She slammed the door.

The bang shook the dust off the shelves. I stood there. The door was cold against my back. I could hear her breathing on the other side. It was fast and shallow.

I realized then that I was not fixing anything. I was just refilling a bucket with a hole in the bottom. Every bit of happiness I poured in drained out at midnight. I was pouring and pouring and the bucket never filled.

I sat down on the floor, my back against the door. The box of posters was next to me. I touched the edge of a poster. It was dusty.

"I can't do this again," I said to the door.
pages.image: Max sits on a garage floor with his back against a closed white door; a cardboard box sits beside him; his head is bowed; dim light from a high window.

pages.text:
Saturdays sixty-eight through seventy felt like running a marathon in a hallway.

I was a butler, a cheerleader, and a therapist, all while being eleven. I snapped at Gus when his roar hit my eardrums at the wrong second. I snapped at Jonah when he thrust his laminated itinerary into my face. I snapped at Dad when he delivered the anti-gravity line for the hundredth time.

"Dad, please," I said on Saturday sixty-nine, holding my head in my hands. "Just say, 'The toast is burnt.'"

He looked genuinely hurt. "But Max, that's the joke."

"I don't care about the joke," I replied, and my voice came out sharp, like a wire being pulled tight.

I looked around the kitchen. The house was quiet. I was the only one who was tired. I was the only one who was working. I was the only one who was unhappy.

A cold shock hit me. The person running the Everyone's Happy program was the most miserable person in the room. I was spending all my energy making everyone else okay, and I was running on fumes.

I wanted one thing back. I wanted to feel good. I wanted the feeling to be mine, not a service I provided to others.
pages.image: Max stands in a kitchen with his hands on his hips, looking angry and tired; Dad stands in the background looking confused and worried; a cardboard box table with a black slice of toast is in the foreground.

pages.text:
Saturday seventy.

I sat on the air mattress in the dark, staring at the bare white ceiling. I had fixed the toast. I had fixed the drums. I had fixed the hugs. But then the clock cuckooed, and all those fixes vanished.

I started thinking about the worst possibility. It settled in my stomach like a heavy rock dropped down a well.

Maybe the wish was a punishment.

Maybe I was being taught a lesson. Perhaps the universe was showing me that I was the kind of person who wanted things to stay exactly the same. That I was selfish. That I was wrong to be angry about leaving. That I was the problem.

It felt worse than being sad. It felt like being accused in court.

I looked at the clock on the wall. It was dark, and the hands were stopped. I did not hear the bird. I just stared at the wood, waiting for the 6:47 roar that would tell me if I was wrong, or right, or just crazy.

The next Saturday was the one I'm least proud of. I'll tell it fast.
pages.image: Max lies on an air mattress in a dark room, staring at a small cuckoo clock on a distant wall; his expression is serious and troubled; faint moonlight from a window.
